## Taxonomic reference

We refer to extant taxa based on their genus and species in the Birds of the World database for consistency (Billerman, 2023). Within data files, taxa are referred to by their name in the data source (Skullsite Bird Skull Collection [Van and Jansen, 2020] or museum specimen designation). Comments in data files note where these identifications differ from Birds of the World or the bird diet database EltonTraits 1.0 (Wilman et al., 2014). Designations and relationships of fossil clades are based on Pittman, 2020b, though use of ‘Bohaiornithidae’ in this work is necessarily imprecise due to the instability of the clade (Table 1, Liu et al., 2022). For reasons explained below, we used Bohaiornithidae to refer to the six taxa referred when the clade was originally defined (Wang, 2014a) plus Beiguornis (Wang, 2022a).

## Taxa included in Bohaiornithidae

The taxa included within Bohaiornithidae vary between studies. A summary of taxa included in the group in multiple phylogenies is provided in Table 1. The original definition of Bohaiornithidae is “the most recent common ancestor of Shenqiornis mengi and Bohaiornis guoi, and all its descendants” (Wang, 2014a), but in practice this definition is used less strictly. Several studies (Wang, 2022a; Figure 3B in Pittman, 2020b; Wang et al., 2015c; Wang and Liu, 2016a) place the Bohaiornithidae node at an earlier diverging position than the strict clade definition in order to include Zhouornis, and others ( Chiappe et al., 2019; Figure 5a in Liu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; O’Connor et al., 2020b) recover Shenqiornis as so early diverging that most or all enantiornithines would be considered bohaiornithids by the strict definition. Liu et al., 2022 call for a redefinition of the clade after these findings, but do not provide a formal one. They place the Bohaiornithidae node on its phylogeny with a set of synapomorphies, but include Gretcheniao and Junornis in the clade which is not supported by subsequent studies (Wang et al., 2022b; Wang, 2022a; Wang et al., 2021b). Overall, the six original taxa proposed as members of Bohaiornithidae by Wang, 2014a tend to be recovered as closely related to Bohaiornis. Longusunguis is recovered in a clade with Bohaiornis in 16 of 22 (73%) studies, Sulcavis and Zhouornis in 18 of 23 (78%), Shenqiornis in 18 of 22 (82%), and Parabohaiornis in 19 of 21 (90%). Conversely, other taxa recovered in Bohaiornithidae tend to only rarely resolve near Bohaiornis. Linyiornis is recovered in a clade with Bohaiornis in 1 of 9 (11%) studies, Eoenantiornis in 3 of 21 (14%), and Fortunguavis in 4 of 19 (21%). Gretcheniao and Musivavis, both described as bohaiornithid-like but not bohaiornithid, are never recovered close to Bohaiornis (closest in Liu et al., 2022, where Gretcheniao is in a clade sister to the six original bohaiornithids plus BMNHC-Ph1204). Beiguornis has only been included in one study (Wang, 2022a), where it is recovered as a bohaiornithid, so it is tentatively included in the group pending future studies.

## Phylogenetic tree topology

Extant bird phylogenetic trees in this study are trimmed versions of the maximum clade credibility supertree used in Cooney et al., 2017. This supertree follows Jetz et al., 2012, a tree time-scaled using Bayesian uncorrelated relaxed molecular clock data from 15 genes in 6663 avian species constrained by seven fossil taxa. These data were mapped onto the backbone of Prum et al., 2015 which used Bayesian uncorrelated relaxed molecular clock data from 259 genes in 200 species constrained by 19 fossil taxa. The tree files and R code to merge them were taken from the supplement of Cooney et al., 2017.

All grafted bohaiornithid branch lengths were scaled linearly so that the total length of the avian portion of the tree was equal to 94 Ma following the estimate of Kuhl et al., 2021. The Ornithothoraces node was placed at 145 Ma after Bayesian morphological clock analysis of two independent character sets (Cau, 2018; Wang et al., 2021a). For the bohaiornithid portion of the tree, a topology recovered by two recent analyses (Wang et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022) was used where Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are sister taxa and the remaining bohaiornithids are in a basal polytomy. The position of Beiguornis is considered uncertain as the phylogeny in its description (Wang, 2022a) differs from this topology, but it was not included in any analyses where phylogeny was incorporated.

## Bohaiornithid fossil dating

Shenqiornis is referred to the Qiaotou Formation (Wang et al., 2010). This has been correlated to the Dawangzhangzi bed of the Yixian Formation (Jin et al., 2008), which is within the ‘Upper Undivided Yixian Formation’ of Zhong et al., 2021 dated to 124 Ma. All other bohaiornithids are referred to the Jiufotang Formation. Most of these (Wang, 2014a; Liu et al., 2022) are from the Xiaotaizi/Lamadong locality dated to 119 Ma (Yu et al., 2021). Longusunguis IVPP V18693 from the Lingyuan locality (Hu et al., 2020b), Zhouornis BMNHC Ph756 from the Xiaoyugou locality (Zhang et al., 2014), and Zhouornis CNUVB 903 of uncertain provenance (Zhang et al., 2013) are referred to 121 Ma as the median age of the Jiufotang Formation (Yu et al., 2021).

## Taxonomic status of BMNHC-Ph1204

BMNHC-Ph1204 was previously identified to Bohaiornithidae indet. (Liu et al., 2022), though we herein refine the diagnosis to cf. Sulcavis. As noted in Liu et al., 2022, the large number of dentary teeth in BMNHC-Ph1204 is only seen in Sulcavis among known bohaiornithids, and the maxillary process of the nasal and interclavicular angle of the specimen are also consistent with those seen in Sulcavis. The final defining feature of BMNHC-Ph1204 noted by Liu et al., 2022 is the lack of a fenestra in the maxilla, and the maxilla is poorly preserved in the Sulcavis holotype with no fenestra visible (O’Connor et al., 2013). Most of the synapomorphies of Sulcavis are present in BMNHC-Ph1204: teeth with a flat lingual margin creating a ‘D-shaped’ cross-section (Liu et al., 2022 p.5); a broad nasal with a short, rostrally directed maxillary process (Liu et al., 2022 p. 3); the caudal-most process of the synsacrum extending far caudally to the vertebra’s articular surface (Figure 8 in Liu et al., 2022); a long and delicate acromion process on the scapula (Figure 7 in Liu et al., 2022); a convex lateral margin of the coracoid (Figure 8 in Liu et al., 2022); and an alular claw larger than that on the major digit (Figure 9 in Liu et al., 2022). The only missing synapomorphy is enamel with longitudinal ridges, autapomorphic for Sulcavis (O’Connor et al., 2013). BMNHC-Ph1204 is less mature than the Sulcavis holotype (Figure 10; O’Connor et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2022), and ontogenetic change in enamel ornamentation has been noted previously in reptiles (Thies and Broschinski, 2001; Street et al., 2021), so it is possible that this is an ontogenetic difference. The same can be said of the additional carpal element in BMNHC-Ph1204, as carpometacarpal fusion is believed to occur relatively late in bohaiornithid ontogeny (Wang, 2014a; Liu et al., 2022). Therefore, with this uncertainty from ontogeny, we refer BMNHC-Ph1204 to cf. Sulcavis. Should this specimen later be referred to its own taxon, the similarities above imply the new taxon would be very closely related to Sulcavis, and this specimen would still be the most appropriate for filling in missing pieces of the skull of Sulcavis, as in Figure 2.

## Bohaiornithid skull reconstruction for MA and FEA

Reconstructions of bohaiornithid skulls are provided in Figure 2. No complete bohaiornithid skulls are currently known, so digital reconstruction was necessary to create workable biological models (Lautenschlager, 2016). Reconstructions of a given taxon used material from that taxon where possible, but each reconstruction required at least one bone from another taxon. Ideally these replacement bones would come from a taxon’s closest relative, but the relationships within Bohaiornithidae are unstable aside from the sister relationship of Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis. For reconstruction purposes, we treated Shenqiornis and Sulcavis as sister taxa due to them having the next most frequent sister pairing among bohaiornithids (Wang et al., 2022b; Zhang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014b) and the superficially similar shallow angle of their rostra. Longusunguis and Zhouornis have the most unstable placement within Bohaiornithidae, so supplemental parts were taken from taxa arbitrarily. Fortunately these taxa each had two moderately complete skulls, so little material from other taxa was needed.

Only Bohaiornis IVPP V17963 preserves the posteroventral region of the skull, so this region in all reconstructions is based on this. This affects jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA) of the upper jaw, and thus this functional index should be interpreted cautiously. We interpret the bone in Bohaiornis LPM B00167 previously labelled as the postorbital (Hu et al., 2011) to be the quadratojugal, as its shape is more similar to the short and weakly forked quadratojugal typical of enantiornithines (Wang and Hu, 2017a) than the elongate postorbital of Longusunguis IVPP V18693 (Hu et al., 2020b), Parabohaiornis IVPP V28398 (Wang, 2023), Sulcavis BMNHC Ph-805 (O’Connor et al., 2013), and cf. Sulcavis BMNHC Ph-1204 (Liu et al., 2022). The alternative is that this bone is in fact the postorbital, meaning Bohaiornis (and possibly Shenqiornis and Zhouornis) lacked a complete postorbital bar.

The jugal and postorbital bones of Longusunguis are elongate and believed to be in contact in life (Hu et al., 2020b), which would increase the overall rigidity and stability of the skull. This is also very likely in Parabohaiornis and Sulcavis, which preserve both a dorsally curving jugal and elongate postorbital (Figure 2C and D). We reconstruct these bones as also in contact in other bohaiornithids (Figure 2A, E and F), though this is less certain. Notably if we are incorrect in our reinterpretation of a bone in LPM B00167 identified as the postorbital (Hu et al., 2011) as the quadratojugal, then this much smaller element could not contact the jugal in life.

## Bohaiornithid ontogeny

Ontogeny is an important dimension to account for when discussing the morphology and ecology of extinct animals, but the ontogeny of Bohaiornithidae (and enantiornithines in general) is poorly understood. Hu and O’Connor, 2017 devised a useful ‘character stage’ system for tracking enantiornithine maturity based on the fusion of compound bones. Bohaiornithids are aged using this framework in Figure 10. Hu and O’Connor, 2017 combine the fusion of the proximal metatarsus, the tibiotarsus, and carpometacarpus into a single stage 3 (presumably due to a lack of resolution). Longusunguis IVPP V18693 has a fused tibiotarsus and unfused tarsometatarsus and carpometacarpus and Sulcavis BMNHC-Ph805 has a fused tibiotarsus and tarsometatarsus but unfused carpometacarpus, indicating the tibiotarsus fused first and the carpometacarpus last within this family. We thus subdivide the stage 3 of Hu and O’Connor, 2017 into 3a (formation of the tibiotarsus), 3b (proximal fusion of the tarsometatarsus), and 3c (fusion of the carpometacarpus) in bohaiornithids.

The above stages only approximate biological maturity, however. Histological data from two bones has been used to suggest that Zhouornis CNUVB-0903 had achieved sexual maturity but not skeletal maturity (Zhang et al., 2013) A recent study (Atterholt et al., 2021) has shown that histological maturity can vary greatly within individual enantiornithines but upholds the diagnosis of CNUVB-0903 as an adult. The indeterminate bohaiornithid CUGB P1202 is considered the least mature published member of the family (Peteya et al., 2017). It was proposed as sexually mature due to its elongate tail feathers (with the assumption they served a sexual display purpose; Peteya et al., 2017), but similar feathers in decidedly juvenile enantiornithines (STM 34-7 [Zheng et al., 2012] and 34-9, IVPP V15564 [O’Connor et al., 2020a]) call this into doubt. By correlating the histological maturity of Atterholt et al., 2021 with the character stage system (Table 10), we see that subadulthood begins at or before character stage 1 and full maturity occurs after completion of character stage 3. We thus consider all bohaiornithids aside from the two mentioned above to be mature subadults or young adults, as proposed previously (Wang, 2014a; Liu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2020b). Most extant animals are considered ‘mature’ upon reaching the subadult stage (Hone et al., 2016), so all specimens examined herein should be adequately mature for comparison to mature extant birds.

## Extant sampling

Extant bird masses were taken from the bird ecology database AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022) and combined with bird diet data from EltonTraits 1.0 Wilman et al., 2014 following the diet cut-offs in Table 2. The mass dataset consists of 8758 birds: 169 folivores, 931 frugivores, 1122 generalists, 475 granivores, 5061 invertivores, 450 nectarivores, 207 piscivores, 35 scavengers, and 308 tetrapod hunters.

No additional extant birds are sampled for MA or FEA beyond the dataset of Miller et al., 2023, meaning these datasets consist of 141 birds: 9 folivores, 17 frugivores, 17 generalists, 8 husking granivores, 8 swallowing granivores, 43 invertivores, 7 nectarivores, 15 piscivores, 8 scavengers, and 9 tetrapod hunters.

Five additional taxa were added to the ungual traditional morphometric (TM) dataset of Miller et al., 2023 to increase the sample of anisodactyl non-raptorial perching birds. Target taxa were identified from the literature as birds with well-recorded perching behaviour and no record of grasping or manipulating prey with the pes. This list of target taxa was sent in a formal loan request to Serina Brady of Carnegie Museum of Natural History, who provided photographs of all available specimens fitting the criteria. In total, the extant TM dataset includes 66 birds: 9 ground birds, 23 non-raptorial perching birds, 4 shrikes, 18 raptors taking large prey, and 12 raptors taking small prey.

Of the 408 extant bird samples included in the skull TM analysis of Clark et al., 2023, 61 were removed due to not meeting the definition of any diet category in Table 2 (they were ‘in between’ diets as defined here, often with 50% of the diet from two sources). Thus, the final skull morphometric dataset consisted of 347 birds across 298 species: 9 folivores, 40 frugivores, 53 generalists, 5 granivores, 175 invertivores, 26 nectarivores, 27 piscivores, 4 scavengers, and 8 tetrapod hunters.

## Analytical techniques

## Body mass

The granivore diet category was not split into husking and swallowing granivores; past work (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023) did not find the two subcategories to meaningfully differ in body mass. Average masses of groups were compared via phylogenetic HSD (pairwise function of R package RRPP [Collyer and Adams, 2018] used to compare group means). Diagnostic cut-off values between groups were found with the R package OptimalCutpoints (López-Ratón, 2014) version 1.1-5 by optimising the Youden index, with bootstrap estimation of 95% confidence intervals using the R package boot (Davison and Hinkley, 1997) version 1.3-28.

## Pedal traditional morphometrics, mechanical advantage, and finite element analysis

The extant MA and FEA data in this study is unchanged from Miller et al., 2023, and new data collected from fossil specimens followed the same procedures as Miller et al., 2023. New fossil MA data were measured from the reconstructions in Figure 2 in CorelDraw X8. FEA models based on the reconstructions in Figure 2 were created and solved within HyperWorks 2022 Student Edition (HyperMesh and Optistruct, Altair Engineering, Inc, USA). We make the assumption that toothed and beaked models are directly comparable given that both operate under constraints of preventing breakage and deformation to the jaw (Miller and Pittman, 2021). Presence of a rhamphotheca is known to reduce stress experienced during a bite (Lautenschlager et al., 2013), so the beaked models all include a modelled rhamphotheca (Miller et al., 2022) to account for this effect. Pedal TM data are measured from scale photographs where available, though the five new included taxa were photographed without scale. All digits from a single individual were measured from a single photograph, so their relative scale is preserved. Our TM data is based solely on angles and length ratios, so this lack of scale should not be an issue. Pedal ecological categories for TM follow Miller et al., 2023; of note, we define raptors taking large prey as those with records of regularly taking prey which cannot be completely encircled by the pes, and raptors taking small prey as those without such records. As pointed out in Fowler et al., 2009, this division commonly follows phylogenetic lines, but we observe exceptions such as B. virginianus taking large prey (Artuso, 2020) and Buteogallus anthracinus not taking large prey (Schnell, 2020) clustering with birds in the same pedal ecological group rather than their phylogenetic relatives. All analyses of the data (PCA, FDA, pFDA, ancestral state reconstruction, etc.) were performed in R version 4.1.2 (R Development Core Team, 2020), with scripts and raw data including measurements and FE models available from Mendeley Data (https://doi.org/10.17632/7xtpbv27zh.3).

## Skull traditional morphometrics

Clark et al., 2023 recently used skull traditional morphometrics to great effect in both differentiating extant bird diets and diagnosing the diet of longipterygid enantiornithines. Thus, we incorporate their data and methodology here as well to expand the evidence supporting our diet diagnoses. Measurements of skull and rostrum length for extant birds are unchanged from Clark et al., 2023. Clark et al., 2023 do not diagram their measurement landmarks, and the caudal landmark of the rostral length as ‘the caudal margin of the lacrimal (i.e. the rostral margin of the orbit)’ does not specify a dorsoventral height. So, for all new rostrum length measurements of bohaiornithids, we measured to the dorsoventral midpoint of the caudal margin of the ventral ramus of the lacrimal.

Diet assignments of extant taxa were changed from those used by Clark et al., 2023 to those in Table 2 for consistency, following information in EltonTraits 1.0 (Wilman et al., 2014). We also use mass estimates for taxa from AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022), rather than those listed by Clark et al., 2023, for consistency within this work.

Clark et al., 2023 visualise (their Figure 4) and generally interpret their skull morphometrics in terms of proportional rostral length (i.e. rostrum length divided by skull length) vs. log10 skull length. We have modified both of these factors in Figure 8. Firstly, we log10-transform both rostrum and skull length before taking their ratio, as this better normalises the distribution of proportional rostral length. Actual distribution of the data along this axis is minimally affected. Secondly, we use a relative skull length instead of absolute skull length. Absolute skull length is essentially a size proxy; Figure 8—figure supplement 1 shows skull length and body mass creating similar distributions, with the position of diet groups maintained relative to one another (while spreading more evenly along the x-axis when using body mass). This work already discusses body size as a diet proxy at length, so including it in morphometric discussion would be redundant. Through log10-log10 regression, we found that skull length generally increases with body mass with a scaling exponent of 2.75 (slightly negative allometry, R2 = 0.63) for the extant birds sampled. Thus we calculated relative skull length as:relativeskulllength=(log10(skulllength))2.7482log10(bodymass)

Relative skull length approximates how much longer or shorter a given bird’s skull is than the expected length for a bird of the same body mass.

## Ancestral state reconstruction

The backbone for the enantiornithine tree topology used in ancestral state reconstruction follows Wang et al., 2021b. This tree contains 34 of the 56 species used in ancestral state reconstruction. Additional taxa were grafted onto this backbone following Wang et al., 2022b; Liu et al., 2022; Wang, 2022a; O’Connor, 2009; Li et al., 2022; O’Connor et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2012a; Kurochkin et al., 2013; and Atterholt et al., 2018. Some taxa have only been included in one phylogenetic analysis, which placed said taxa within Bohaiornithidae, Longipterygidae, or Pengornithidae (e.g. Noguerornis placed within Longipterygidae by O’Connor, 2009). These taxa all lack the synapomorphies used to formally define the relevant clade, and their placements within them are likely artefacts of sharing a few characters while most data are missing. We therefore maintained monophyly of Bohaiornithidae, Longipterygidae, and Pengornithidae by placing these ambiguous taxa as sister to the family they were placed within. Time-scaling was performed using the R package paleotree (Bapst, 2012). All enantiornithine taxa were placed at their earliest occurrence, with species divergence arbitrarily chosen to take 1000 years. The enantiornithine phylogeny was rooted at 144 Ma after Cau, 2018 and Wang et al., 2021a. Ages of localities follow Zhong et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2006; Fregenal-Martínez, 2017; Lockley et al., 2018; Porfiri et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Napoli et al., 2021; Galobart et al., 2022; Montano et al., 2022; and Ramezani et al., 2022, with precise notes in the data repository (https://doi.org/10.17632/7xtpbv27zh.3). If the horizon of a specimen was in doubt, it was placed at the median age of the formation.

The diet of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes was reconstructed in two ways: qualitatively, directly labelling diets onto taxa to reconstruct the diet of ancestral nodes; and quantitatively, reconstructing ancestral body mass, jaw MA and functional indices, jaw FEA MWAM strain and interval values, and pedal TM values, and predicting ancestral diet from these reconstructed values. The qualitative set includes quantitative diet reconstructions made here, quantitative reconstructions from Miller et al., 2022 and Miller et al., 2023, all qualitative hypotheses of diet in enantiornithines (Table 11), and all enantiornithines with mass data (approximating enantiornithines known from substantial fossil material, as they need to be somewhat complete for mass estimation; Cuspirostrisornis, Dalingheornis, Gracilornis, Jibeinia, Longchengornis, Microenantiornis, and Paraprotopteryx were excluded due to never being included in a phylogenetic analysis). The latter were coded with ‘Unknown’ diet to illustrate uncertainty in the reconstruction. As hypothesised diets are less precise than the diet categories used elsewhere in this study, they were lumped together as herbivores (folivores, frugivores, granivores, and nectarivores), invertivores, omnivores (generalists), or vertivores (piscivores, tetrapod hunters, and scavengers). In total, 14 of 30 (47%) of diets in this reconstruction are supported by preserved meal evidence or quantitative diet proxies. A total of 56 taxa are included in the qualitative ancestral state reconstruction.

Quantitative ancestral state reconstruction includes data from the present study and our two other quantitative analyses of enantiornithines (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023), as well as pedal TM data for Fortunguavis from Pittman et al., 2022 and mass data from Miller and Pittman, 2021 and Serrano et al., 2015. Only MWAM strain of FEA models was reconstructed, not full intervals data, as we found the validity of reconstructing an individual strain interval to be dubious. If pedal TM data was available for multiple specimens of a genus, we favoured the most mature specimen to represent the genus. If mass data was available for multiple specimens of a genus, we favoured the largest mass estimate as an assumption of it representing the most mature sample. The large-toothed Longipteryx morphotype (Miller et al., 2022) was assumed more mature than the small-toothed morphotype and used for all reconstructions. A total of 44 taxa are used in ancestral state reconstruction of body mass, 13 in upper jaw MA, 9 in lower jaw MA, 13 in FEA, and 16 in pedal TM.

Sapeornis was used as the outgroup in ancestral state reconstruction. Mass data for the taxon was taken from Serrano et al., 2015. MA data was measured from the reconstruction in Hu et al., 2020a. FEA data was taken from a model constructed by Yuen Ting (Athena) Tse for an in-progress collaborative work based on the same reconstruction (Hu et al., 2020a). TM data were taken from Pittman et al., 2022. Its qualitative diet was classified as herbivorous based on preserved seed meals (O’Connor, 2019a). Its divergence from Enantiornithes was placed at 147 Ma after Wang et al., 2021a.

Ancestral states were estimated using the fastAnc() function in Phytools 0.7-90 (Revell, 2012). As polytomies are present in the enantiornithine tree used, ancestral states were calculated 10,000 times with random resolutions of the polytomies and averaged. As some diets were uncertain (e.g. Zhouornis may be either herbivorous or a generalist), and fastAnc() cannot accept probabilistic qualitative states for terminal taxa, we coded diets quantitatively as percent likelihood for each diet.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa1)

Understanding the ecology including the dietary ecology of enantiornithines is challenging by all means. This work explores the possible trophic diversity of the "opposite-bird" enantiornithines by referring to the body mass, jaw mechanical advantage, finite element analysis of the jaw bones, and morphometrics of the claws and skull of both fossil and extant avian species. By incorporation the dietary information of longipterygids and pengornithinds, the authors predicted a wide variety of foods for enantiornithine ancestors. This indicates the evolutionary successes of enantiornitine during Cretaceous is very likely to have been driven by the wide range of recipes. I believe this work represented the most comprehensive analysis of enantiornithines' diet and trophic diversity by far and the first systematic dietary analysis of bohaiornithids, though the analysis themselves are largely based on the indirect evidence including jaw bone morphologies and claw and skull morphometrics. Anyway, I believe the authors did most the paleontologists could do, and I do not know whether the conclusions could be further supported by incorporating some geochemical data, as most of the specimens the authors analyzed were recovered from a small geographic area. The results also indicate that the developmental trajectories of enantiornithines, at least for jaw bones, might also have been diverse to some extent in response to the diverse ecological niches they adapted. My only concern regarding the analysis is to what extent the conclusions are convincing by comparing specimens representing various ontogenetic stages. This concern has been addressed in the revised manuscript. I believe the authors have almost exhausted all available methods, and I congratulate the authors for the detailed study they conducted.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89871.3.sa3)

Summary:

The authors use several quantitative approaches to characterize the feeding ecologies of bohaiornithid enantiornithines, including allometric data, mechanical advantage and finite element analyses of the jaw, and morphometric analyses of the claws. The authors combine their results with data for other enantiornithines collected from the literature to shed new insight on the ecological evolution of Enantiornithes as a clade.

Although the authors have taken steps to improve their paper, I generally find improvements unsatisfying, especially regarding my comments.

My remaining concerns:

Teeth: My concern here is not whether having teeth limits available niche space compared to having a keratinous beak. Rather, my concern regards how exploitation of the same niche space might be differently reflected in parameter space between birds with teeth and birds with beaks. Can we reliably expect two species that both eat seeds to occupy the same parameter space if, for example, distribution of stress/strain is across a series of teeth vs. across a more uniform beak? In this manuscript, the authors are clearly making this assumption, but that assumption is not made explicit, let alone justified. The authors should discuss this.

Cranial kinesis: As with teeth, my concern here regards our ability to compare data between birds with and without a flexible beak to mitigate forces when foraging. I appreciate that the functional complexity of the kinetic neognath skull precludes our ability to account for it in analyses such as these, but when comparisons are made using these analyses *specifically among neognaths*, we can reliably assume that we are comparing like to like - that is, we can assume that both have kinetic skulls, and so kinesis is reflected similarly in the data for each bird. Similarly, even if a comparison between two neognaths focuses exclusively on the mandible - in which cranial kinesis is not directly reflected - we can assume that those mandibles serve as comparisons between functionally similar systems. However, we cannot necessarily make those same assumptions when comparing the kinetic skull of a neognath to the akinetic skull of an enantiornithine. Indeed, even when focusing just on the mandible, can we reliably assume that data collected from an akinetic enantiornithine reflect the same comparative context as data collected from kinetic neognaths? I appreciate that the authors added a call for better functional understanding of bird cranial kinesis - a call I enthusiastically endorse - but the authors should still discuss how that current lack of understanding impacts interpretations of the comparisons they draw.

Finally, I still find the discussion to be overly long and lacking clear focus and organization. I again urge the authors to minimally consider adding subheadings to better allow the reader to follow the flow of ideas, and I second Reviewer #1's suggestion to add a "Conclusions" section.

results.result: Bohaiornis is identified as herbivorous, specifically folivorous, based on multiple lines of evidence. The taxon has a body mass of 91-406 g (mean 248 g excluding outliers), low jaw-closing mechanical advantage but distinctly high jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA), and jaw strength under FEA loading similar to folivores. The hoatzin and southern screamer are proposed as extant analogues.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29-C30, C32-C33, C35-C36, and C51-C54 collectively provide converging evidence from body mass, mechanical advantage, FEA, and skull morphometrics that support a folivorous diet for Bohaiornis. The high OMA is particularly diagnostic for folivory, and the comparison to extant analogues with similar functional traits strengthens this interpretation.

results.result: Parabohaiornis is identified as herbivorous with affinities to both swallowing granivores and folivores. Body mass estimates range from 178-406 g, with mechanical advantage and FEA results showing similarity to swallowing granivores and folivores. Sandgrouse are proposed as a potential extant analogue.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29-C30, C32, C55-C56 provide multiple lines of evidence supporting herbivory in Parabohaiornis, though the diagnosis is less clear than for Bohaiornis. The body mass, MA, and FEA data consistently point to plant-eating adaptations, though the specific type of herbivory (granivory vs. folivory) remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Longusunguis is identified as a raptorial carnivore adapted for taking large prey. The taxon plots among large raptors in pedal traditional morphometric analysis and possesses more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids, a feature associated with carnivory.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C38, C63-C64 provide converging evidence from pedal morphometrics and dental morphology supporting raptorial carnivory in Longusunguis. The consistent recovery of this taxon with large raptors in multiple analyses and the presence of recurved teeth strengthen this interpretation.

results.result: Zhouornis is identified as either frugivorous or a generalist feeder. It has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids (89-156 µε MWAM strain) and is the largest bohaiornithid (mean estimate 758 g for largest specimen). The barred owl is proposed as having similar body mass and claw shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C29-C30, C35-C36, and C60-C62 provide multiple lines of evidence supporting either frugivory or generalist feeding in Zhouornis. The exceptionally strong jaw, large body mass, and intermediate pedal morphology are consistent with both dietary interpretations, though the evidence does not definitively distinguish between them.

results.result: Shenqiornis and Sulcavis have uncertain diets, with piscivory, generalist feeding, and folivory all plausible. Body mass data can only rule out granivory, invertivory, and nectarivory.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C29-C30 indicate that multiple lines of evidence fail to provide clear dietary resolution for these taxa. The intermediate values across multiple proxies and reliance on reconstructed skull material for Shenqiornis create substantial uncertainty. Additional specimens and analytical approaches are needed.

results.result: Body mass in extant birds separates into four significantly different diet groups with specific cut-off values: nectarivores (<9 g), granivores/invertivores (9-56 g), frugivores/generalists (56-265 g), and folivores/tetrapod hunters (>265 g). Significant phylogenetic signal (K=0.93) was found in extant bird mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 and C31 describe a well-supported statistical analysis of body mass and diet relationships in 8758 extant birds. The use of phylogenetic HSD and optimization of the Youden index with bootstrap confidence intervals provides robust support for the identified cut-off values and phylogenetic signal.

results.result: Bohaiornithids generally have low jaw-closing mechanical advantage (AMA, PMA) and relative jaw dimensions (AO, MMH) compared to living birds. Most have low jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA) except Bohaiornis which has high OMA. Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant MA dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 describe mechanical advantage measurements from reconstructed skulls with clear patterns distinguishing Bohaiornis from other bohaiornithids. The phylogenetic signal in extant data supports the validity of the comparative framework, though the authors note that MA has poor predictive power for diet in extant birds.

results.result: Bohaiornithid jaws show low MWAM strain (89-156 µε, mean 128 µε) under FEA loading, with Bohaiornis and Zhouornis experiencing less strain than any extant carnivorous bird. No significant phylogenetic signal was recovered in extant FEA data.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 describe FEA results showing bohaiornithids have stronger jaws than previously studied enantiornithine families. The lack of phylogenetic signal in extant FEA data is noted as limiting the predictive power of this approach, but the comparative strength measurements are well-supported by the modeling.

results.result: Pedal traditional morphometric analysis shows Sulcavis plotting among large raptors, both Parabohaiornis individuals among non-raptorial perching birds, and significant phylogenetic signal in the extant dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 describe pedal TM results from PCA analysis. The phylogenetic signal supports the validity of the comparative framework. However, the interpretation of Sulcavis as raptorial is complicated by its unusual digit proportions (enlarged digit I without enlarged opposing digit), creating some uncertainty about functional interpretation.

results.result: Skull traditional morphometric analysis shows that granivores and tetrapod hunters have short rostra (<0.8), folivores/nectarivores/piscivores have elongate rostra (>0.8), and nectarivores (specifically hummingbirds) have distinctly elongate skulls (>4.5). Bohaiornithids display distinctly short skulls (<1.6), with Zhouornis having the shortest skull relative to body mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 describe skull TM patterns in extant birds and bohaiornithids. However, the authors note that bohaiornithids do not conform to the general correlation between rostrum and skull length seen in extant birds (C134), suggesting different developmental constraints may be at play. This limits the interpretive power of skull TM for bohaiornithids.

results.result: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts the common ancestor of Enantiornithes was an arboreal generalist feeder with body mass near 200 g, jaw strain of 227 µε, and claw shape intermediate between non-raptorial perchers and shrikes. Ancestral states for major enantiornithine families show varying levels of certainty.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C46-C50, and C75-C78 describe ancestral state reconstructions, but the authors explicitly note high uncertainty (99% unknown for common ancestor of all Enantiornithes and Pengornithidae). The reconstruction is heavily influenced by which taxa are included and their phylogenetic positions. The authors acknowledge that only 47% of diets in the qualitative reconstruction are supported by direct evidence (C107), limiting confidence in ancestral state estimates.

results.result: Bohaiornithids cover greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families (Longipterygidae and Pengornithidae). This increased dietary breadth appears to stem from increased jaw strength, with a stepwise increase across families: longipterygids weakest (259-345 µε), pengornithids intermediate (190-275 µε), and bohaiornithids strongest (89-156 µε).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 describe a clear pattern of increasing jaw strength and dietary diversity across enantiornithine families. The FEA data showing stepwise increases in jaw strength are well-supported, and the correlation with dietary diversity is logical. However, the authors note that poor resolution of relationships within Bohaiornithidae limits testing of whether skull strengthening drove diversification.

results.result: Enantiornithines achieved ecological diversity comparable to crown birds within 25 million years (by 120 Ma), faster than crown birds achieved similar diversity after the K-Pg extinction. This suggests traits unique to crown birds (edentulism, cranial kinesis) cannot fully explain their ecological success.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C79-C83 present a comparative evolutionary argument based on the timing of diversification. The 25-million-year timeframe for enantiornithine diversification is well-supported by the dietary diversity documented in this study and the phylogenetic dating. The comparison to crown bird diversification timelines is appropriately cited (C81), supporting the conclusion that crown bird traits are not necessary for rapid ecological diversification.

results.result: Previous hypotheses of bohaiornithid durophagy are evaluated and found to be only partially supported. Bohaiornithids have robust teeth and stronger jaws than other enantiornithines, but lack the extreme jaw-closing mechanical advantage and jaw strength of extant durophages (husking granivores and parrots).
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C119, and C124 address prior hypotheses about bohaiornithid diet. The evaluation is well-supported by quantitative comparisons to extant durophages showing that while bohaiornithids have relatively strong jaws, they fall short of the adaptations seen in birds that regularly crack hard seeds and nuts. The authors appropriately refine the durophagy hypothesis rather than simply rejecting it.

results.result: Despite the inferred absence of crops and gizzards in enantiornithines, herbivory in Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis could be sustained through oral processing with robust teeth and/or specialized hindgut fermentation. Plant propagules preserved in the hindgut region of seven enantiornithine specimens support the possibility of hindgut specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59, C119-C120 present a speculative but plausible mechanism for herbivory in enantiornithines. The preservation of plant propagules in the hindgut region (C59) provides some support, but the authors acknowledge this is indirect evidence. The comparison to extant herbivorous birds with hindgut specialization is appropriate, but the absence of direct evidence for such structures in enantiornithines limits confidence.

results.result: No complete bohaiornithid skulls are known, requiring digital reconstruction. Only Bohaiornis IVPP V17963 preserves the posteroventral skull region, which was used for all reconstructions. The quadrate is disarticulated in all specimens, and sensitivity analysis shows folivory cannot be ruled out for any bohaiornithid regardless of quadrate position.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 and C117-C118 describe important methodological limitations and how they were addressed. The sensitivity analysis of quadrate position (C118) is a strength of the study, showing that the main conclusions are robust to uncertainty in skull reconstruction. However, this also highlights the inherent uncertainty in functional interpretations based on reconstructed fossils.

results.result: The original pedal TM dataset was biased toward zygodactyl and semi-zygodactyl non-raptorial perching birds. Five additional anisodactyl taxa were added, but this had minimal effect on results. Toe arrangement is concluded not to be a driving force of the observed trends.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C140 describe an important methodological refinement in response to a valid criticism. The addition of anisodactyl taxa and demonstration that results are robust to this change strengthens confidence in the pedal TM analysis. The conclusion that toe arrangement is not a major driver is well-supported by the minimal change in results and the distribution of semi-zygodactyl taxa.

results.result: The hypothesis of Longipteryx as a specialist piscivore can no longer be rejected based on refined mass data showing three specimens above the mass cut-off for piscivory.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 represents a revision of the authors' previous conclusion based on improved body mass data. The refined analysis with a larger sample size (8758 vs. previous smaller datasets) provides a more robust mass-diet relationship, supporting this revision. However, the authors note that MA results still indicate piscivory is not particularly likely, creating some tension in the evidence.

results.result: Bohaiornithid tooth shape is proposed to be driven by phylogeny rather than diet, with robust teeth potentially serving as general-use tools for processing diverse foods rather than adaptations to a specialized diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 present an alternative interpretation of bohaiornithid tooth morphology based on the dietary diversity documented in this study. The inference that similar tooth shapes across taxa with different diets indicates phylogenetic rather than dietary signal is logical. However, C126 is explicitly speculative, and the functional significance of tooth robustness remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Bohaiornithid claw curvature and size are generally conserved through ontogeny. Ontogenetic staging based on bone fusion and histology indicates that most specimens examined are mature subadults or young adults, appropriate for comparison to mature extant birds.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C141-C145 address an important consideration for functional morphology studies. The correlation of character stages with histological maturity (C144) and the conclusion that most specimens are adequately mature for comparison (C145) are well-supported. This justifies the inclusion of specimens at different ontogenetic stages in the analyses.

results.result: The study uses extensive comparative datasets: 8758 birds for body mass, 141 birds for MA and FEA, 66 birds for pedal TM, and 347 birds for skull TM. These datasets span multiple diet categories and ecological groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 and C100-C103 describe the comparative datasets used in the study. The sample sizes are substantial, particularly for body mass (8758 birds), providing robust comparative frameworks. The smaller samples for MA, FEA, and TM are appropriate given the more intensive data collection required for these methods.

results.result: BMNHC-Ph1204 is referred to cf. Sulcavis based on multiple shared synapomorphies including tooth morphology, nasal structure, synsacrum morphology, and limb proportions.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 describes a taxonomic refinement based on detailed morphological comparison. The identification of multiple shared synapomorphies provides strong support for referring this specimen to cf. Sulcavis. The authors appropriately note uncertainty due to ontogenetic differences, justifying the 'cf.' designation.

results.result: The authors claim that Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds based on mechanical advantage (MA), finite element analysis (FEA), and skull morphometric analyses. Bohaiornis shows high jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA) and jaw strength similar to folivores, with the hoatzin and southern screamer as extant analogues. Parabohaiornis shows herbivorous affinities with similarity to swallowing granivores like sandgrouse.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges this work as 'the most comprehensive analysis of enantiornithines' diet and trophic diversity by far' and states the authors 'did most the paleontologists could do.' The editor describes the study as 'important' with 'a large amount of data' forming 'a solid dataset.' No reviewer challenges the herbivorous interpretations for these taxa.

results.result: The authors claim that Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores based on pedal traditional morphometric analysis showing affinity with large raptors in PCA, along with more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids, which are associated with carnivory.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 congratulates the authors for their 'detailed study' and notes no specific concerns about the raptorial interpretation of Longusunguis. Reviewer 2 approves the revised manuscript. The carnivorous interpretation is accepted as part of the overall dietary diversity findings.

results.result: The authors claim that Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders, having the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids and being the largest bohaiornithid (mean estimate 758 g for the largest specimen), with the barred owl as a similar extant analogue.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges the comprehensive nature of the analysis and raises no concerns about the Zhouornis dietary interpretation. Reviewer 2 approves the revised manuscript. The interpretation is accepted as part of the broader finding of bohaiornithid ecological diversity.

results.result: The authors claim that Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both based on MA and FEA analyses showing affinities with multiple diet groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes this work represents 'the most comprehensive analysis' and raises no concerns about these ambiguous dietary assignments. The reviewers accept that some taxa show mixed signals consistent with generalist or varied diets.

results.result: The authors predict the ancestral enantiornithine bird was a generalist which ate a wide variety of foods, based on ancestral state reconstruction showing body mass near 200 g, jaw strain of 227 µε, and claw shape plotting between non-raptorial perchers and shrikes, indicating an arboreal generalist feeder.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'predicted a wide variety of foods for enantiornithine ancestors' and finds this indicates 'evolutionary successes of enantiornitine during Cretaceous is very likely to have been driven by the wide range of recipes.' Reviewer 2 finds the ancestral generalist proposal 'curious, thought-provoking' and approves the manuscript.

results.result: The authors claim that by the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction, achieving this diversity in only 25 million years. They argue that traits unique to crown birds like edentulism or cranial kinesis cannot fully explain crown bird ecological success, and that crown birds may have been slower to occupy the same ecological breadth.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 finds 'the idea that enantiornithines had occupied a similar niche breadth to post-K-Pg derived birds to be a curious, thought-provoking proposal' and approves the manuscript. The editor notes the article 'will be of interest to colleagues studying...the impact of the mass extinction event 66 million years ago.' This major comparative conclusion is accepted by reviewers.

results.result: The authors claim that bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families (longipterygids and pengornithids), with this increased dietary breadth stemming from increased skull strength. They show a stepwise increase in jaw strength: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε), pengornithids are stronger (190–275 µε), and bohaiornithids are stronger still (89–156 µε).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states this work is 'the first systematic dietary analysis of bohaiornithids' and represents 'the most comprehensive analysis of enantiornithines' diet and trophic diversity by far.' The comparative framework across families is accepted as a key contribution showing progressive ecological diversification.

results.result: The authors present body mass analysis showing that bird masses separate into four significantly different diet category combinations with specific cut-off points (9 g, 56 g, 265 g), and that bohaiornithid body masses range from 91 g to 905 g (mean 287 g). Significant phylogenetic signal was found in extant bird mass (K = 0.93).
results.evaluation: The editor notes 'the large amount of data the authors collected forms a solid dataset.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the comprehensive nature of the analysis. The body mass data and statistical analyses are accepted as foundational to the dietary interpretations.

results.result: The authors report that bohaiornithids generally have low anterior and posterior jaw-closing mechanical advantage (AMA, PMA), relative articular offset (AO), and relative maximum mandibular height (MMH) relative to living birds, though Bohaiornis has a high jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA). Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant MA dataset.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the analysis is based on 'jaw bone morphologies' and represents comprehensive work. The MA data are accepted as part of the multi-proxy approach to dietary reconstruction, with no specific concerns raised about the measurements or interpretations.

results.result: The authors report that bohaiornithid MWAM strain is low (89–156 µε, mean 128 µε), with Bohaiornis and Zhouornis experiencing less strain under loading than any extant carnivorous bird in the study (min = 105 µε). No significant phylogenetic signal was recovered in the extant FEA data.
results.evaluation: The editor describes the dataset as 'solid' and Reviewer 1 acknowledges the FEA as part of the comprehensive analytical approach. The FEA results are accepted as supporting the dietary interpretations, particularly for strong-jawed taxa.

results.result: The authors report that both Parabohaiornis individuals plot among non-raptorial perching birds in pedal TM PCA, with significant phylogenetic signal present in the dataset. They added five additional anisodactyl taxa to address concerns about toe arrangement, finding minimal effect on results, and conclude that toe arrangement is not a driving force of the observed trends.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors addressed concerns about ontogenetic stages in the revised manuscript. The pedal morphometric data and the response to concerns about toe arrangement are accepted, with reviewers approving the revised analyses.

results.result: The authors report skull morphometric patterns showing that granivores and tetrapod hunters have relatively short rostra while folivores, nectarivores, and piscivores have elongate rostra. Bohaiornithids display distinctly short skulls (relative skull length <1.6), with Zhouornis having the shortest skull relative to body mass. Unlike extant birds where rostrum elongation parallels skull elongation, bohaiornithids show the opposite pattern.
results.evaluation: The editor notes the methods 'might in principle be extensible to other limbed vertebrates' and the dataset is 'solid.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the skull morphometrics as part of the comprehensive analysis. The skull shape data are accepted as contributing to dietary interpretations.

results.result: The authors present ancestral state reconstruction results showing the common ancestor of Avisauridae as 100% likely a vertivore, Bohaiornithidae as 34% herbivore/33% vertivore/33% omnivore, Longipterygidae as 100% invertivore, and both Pengornithidae and all Enantiornithes as 99% unknown.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'predicted a wide variety of foods for enantiornithine ancestors' based on incorporating dietary information across families. Reviewer 2 approves the manuscript including the ancestral state reconstructions. The uncertainty for some nodes is accepted as reflecting limited data.

results.result: The authors describe their comparative datasets including nearly 200 extant birds for MA/FEA, expanded to 8758 birds for mass analysis using AVONET, 66 birds for pedal TM, and 347 birds across 298 species for skull morphometrics.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'the large amount of data the authors collected forms a solid dataset.' Reviewer 1 notes this represents 'the most comprehensive analysis' to date. The extensive comparative datasets are accepted as a strength of the study.

results.result: The authors note that no complete bohaiornithid skulls are currently known, requiring digital reconstruction. The quadrate is disarticulated in every published bohaiornithid skull, but sensitivity analysis of quadrate position indicates that folivory cannot be ruled out for any bohaiornithid.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges the authors 'did most the paleontologists could do' given the limitations of fossil material. The editor notes 'concerns regarding some of the details' of methods but accepts the overall approach. The reconstruction methodology and sensitivity analyses are accepted as appropriate given fossil preservation.

results.result: The authors describe their methodological approaches including mechanical advantage analysis for bite speed/force trade-offs, FEA principles for assessing shape strength, and traditional morphometrics of claw curvature to differentiate raptorial from non-raptorial birds. They acknowledge that the extent of upper beak excursion during biting is unrecorded for most taxa.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises persistent concerns about comparing data between toothed enantiornithines and beaked neognaths, stating 'my concern regards how exploitation of the same niche space might be differently reflected in parameter space between birds with teeth and birds with beaks' and that 'the authors are clearly making this assumption, but that assumption is not made explicit, let alone justified.' This methodological concern about comparability remains unresolved.

results.result: The authors argue that bohaiornithids have some of the most robust teeth within Enantiornithes, but do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant durophages. They suggest bohaiornithid tooth shape is driven by phylogeny rather than diet, with robust teeth serving as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3's concern about comparing toothed and beaked birds directly impacts this interpretation: 'Can we reliably expect two species that both eat seeds to occupy the same parameter space if, for example, distribution of stress/strain is across a series of teeth vs. across a more uniform beak?' This fundamental methodological question affects the tooth function interpretations.

results.result: The authors note that presence of a rhamphotheca is known to reduce stress experienced during a bite, citing Lautenschlager et al., 2013.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 expresses concern about cranial kinesis comparisons: 'my concern here regards our ability to compare data between birds with and without a flexible beak to mitigate forces when foraging' and notes 'we cannot necessarily make those same assumptions when comparing the kinetic skull of a neognath to the akinetic skull of an enantiornithine.' This affects interpretations involving beak mechanics.

results.result: The authors address ontogenetic concerns by citing histological data showing Zhouornis CNUVB-0903 achieved sexual but not skeletal maturity, correlating histological maturity with character stages to show subadulthood begins at or before character stage 1 and full maturity occurs after stage 3.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'My only concern regarding the analysis is to what extent the conclusions are convincing by comparing specimens representing various ontogenetic stages. This concern has been addressed in the revised manuscript.' The ontogenetic considerations are accepted as adequately addressed.

results.result: The authors establish context that enantiornithines were the dominant, most abundant and speciose birds of the Mesozoic/Cretaceous, but understanding of their diet remains tenuous with only 12 of over 100 species examined, and dietary evolution in birds outside the crown is poorly understood.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as an 'important study' addressing 'surprisingly diverse diets of a group of toothed birds that lived over 100 million years ago.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'understanding the ecology including the dietary ecology of enantiornithines is challenging by all means.' The knowledge gap motivating the study is accepted.

comparisons.comparison: Both support herbivorous/folivorous interpretations for Bohaiornis (C4, C51-C54). OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of converging evidence from multiple proxies. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'the most comprehensive analysis' with no challenges to herbivorous interpretations.

Both support herbivory in Parabohaiornis (C4, C55-C56). OpenEval notes less diagnostic clarity than Bohaiornis but multiple supporting lines of evidence. Peer reviewers accept herbivorous interpretations without specific concerns.

Perfect alignment on raptorial carnivory in Longusunguis (C5, C38, C63-C64). Both find converging evidence from pedal morphometrics and dental morphology well-supported. Peer reviewers congratulate authors on detailed study with no concerns.

Both support frugivory/generalist interpretation for Zhouornis (C6, C60-C62). OpenEval notes evidence doesn't definitively distinguish between dietary modes. Peer reviewers accept as part of comprehensive analysis showing bohaiornithid diversity.

Both acknowledge dietary uncertainty for some taxa (C7). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to intermediate values and reconstructed material. Peer reviewers accept ambiguous assignments as reflecting generalist or varied diets.

Both support body mass analysis and statistical methods (C25-C28, C31). OpenEval emphasizes robust phylogenetic HSD and bootstrap confidence intervals. Peer reviewers describe dataset as 'solid' and foundational to dietary interpretations.

Perfect agreement on mechanical advantage measurements (C32-C34). Both note clear patterns distinguishing Bohaiornis despite limited predictive power for diet in extant birds. Peer reviewers accept MA as part of comprehensive multi-proxy approach.

Perfect agreement on FEA results (C35-C37). Both support findings that bohaiornithids have stronger jaws than other enantiornithine families. Peer reviewers accept FEA despite lack of phylogenetic signal in extant data.

Both support pedal morphometric analysis (C39-C40, C137-C140). OpenEval notes phylogenetic signal validates framework but uncertainty about Sulcavis. Peer reviewers accept revised analysis addressing toe arrangement concerns.

Both support skull morphometric patterns (C41-C45). OpenEval notes bohaiornithids don't conform to extant correlations, limiting interpretive power. Peer reviewers accept skull shape data as contributing to dietary interpretations.

Divergent evaluations of ancestral state reconstructions (C8, C46-C50, C75-C78). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to high uncertainty and only 47% direct evidence support. Peer reviewers find ancestral generalist proposal 'curious, thought-provoking' and SUPPORTED.

OpenEval rates ancestral reconstructions UNCERTAIN (C46-C50) noting heavy influence of taxon sampling. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the reconstructions, accepting uncertainty for some nodes as reflecting limited data.

Perfect agreement on progressive jaw strengthening and dietary diversification across families (C65-C71). Both support clear stepwise pattern in FEA data. Peer reviewers accept as key contribution showing ecological diversification.

Perfect agreement on comparative evolutionary argument (C9, C79-C83). Both support 25-million-year diversification timeframe and comparison to crown birds. Peer reviewers find proposal 'curious, thought-provoking' with implications for K-Pg extinction studies.

Divergent evaluations of durophagy hypothesis refinement (C16-C17, C119, C124). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on quantitative comparisons. Peer reviewer R17 rates UNCERTAIN due to fundamental concerns about comparing toothed vs. beaked birds.

OpenEval rates herbivory mechanism (C57-C59, C119-C120) as UNCERTAIN due to indirect evidence and speculation about hindgut specialization. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific mechanistic claim.

Perfect agreement on methodological limitations and sensitivity analyses (C96-C97, C117-C118). Both support reconstruction methodology as appropriate given fossil preservation. Peer reviewers note authors 'did most paleontologists could do.'

Both support pedal analysis refinements (C137-C140). OpenEval emphasizes robustness to anisodactyl taxa addition. Peer reviewers explicitly state ontogenetic concerns 'have been addressed in the revised manuscript.'

OpenEval supports revision of piscivory conclusion for specific taxon (C113) based on improved body mass data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific taxonomic revision.

Divergent evaluations of tooth morphology interpretations (C125-C126). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED that similar teeth across different diets indicates phylogenetic signal. Peer reviewer R17 rates UNCERTAIN due to concerns about comparing toothed vs. beaked birds.

Strong agreement on ontogenetic considerations (C99, C141-C145). Both support conclusion that specimens are adequately mature for comparison. Peer reviewer explicitly states 'This concern has been addressed in the revised manuscript.'

Perfect agreement on comparative dataset quality (C23-C24, C100-C103). Both emphasize substantial sample sizes provide robust frameworks. Peer reviewers explicitly state 'large amount of data forms a solid dataset.'
OpenEval supports taxonomic refinement for cf. Sulcavis specimen (C112) based on shared synapomorphies. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific taxonomic assignment.

Peer reviewer R16 rates UNCERTAIN the fundamental assumption of comparing toothed enantiornithines to beaked neognaths (C116, C20-C22), stating assumption 'is not made explicit, let alone justified.' No corresponding OpenEval result addresses this methodological concern.

Peer reviewer R18 rates UNCERTAIN the comparability of kinetic vs. akinetic skulls (C104), noting 'we cannot necessarily make those same assumptions when comparing the kinetic skull of a neognath to the akinetic skull of an enantiornithine.' No corresponding OpenEval result addresses this concern.

Peer reviewers accept the knowledge gap and study motivation (C1-C2, C12-C14) as important, describing work as addressing 'surprisingly diverse diets' and acknowledging dietary ecology is 'challenging by all means.' No corresponding OpenEval result evaluates study motivation claims.
